what_its_for: Ziprasidone is used to treat schizophrenia (a mental health condition that affects how you think, feel, and behave) and bipolar disorder (extreme mood swings including mania). It helps reduce symptoms like hallucinations, delusions, and severe mood episodes so you can feel more like yourself and function better in daily life.
how_to_take: Take ziprasidone capsules by mouth TWICE a day WITH FOOD. This is very important — taking it without food can mean your body does not absorb the medicine properly, and it may not work as well. Swallow the capsules whole. Do not crush, chew, or open them. Try to take it at the same times each day (for example, with breakfast and dinner) to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it based on how you respond and how well you tolerate the medicine. Typical doses range from 40 mg to 160 mg per day, split into two doses. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose on your own, even if you feel better.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if it is still close to the time you were supposed to take it. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store ziprasidone capsules at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the medicine in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Store it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking ziprasidone, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require sharp focus until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid overheating and dehydration — ziprasidone can affect your body's ability to cool itself, so drink plenty of water, especially in hot weather or during exercise. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may interact with this medicine. Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, because many medications can interact with ziprasidone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: an irregular or fast heartbeat, fainting, or feel like your heart is pounding (these could be signs of a serious heart rhythm problem); high fever, stiff muscles, confusion, or sweating (signs of a rare but serious condition called Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome); uncontrolled movements of your face, tongue, or body (a condition called tardive dyskinesia); signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurred vision; thoughts of harming yourself or others; severe dizziness when standing up; or a skin rash or allergic reaction. Also tell your doctor if you feel more anxious, agitated, or notice any unusual changes in your mood or behavior.
when_it_works: You may notice some improvement in sleep and anxiety within the first few days. However, it usually takes 2 to 4 weeks to notice meaningful changes in your symptoms. For full benefit, it may take several weeks to a few months. It is very important to keep taking the medicine every day even if you do not feel any different right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, as stopping suddenly can make your condition worse.
special_populations: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis should NOT take ziprasidone, as it can increase the risk of death in this group. Pregnant women should talk to their doctor before taking this medicine, as it may cause muscle stiffness or withdrawal symptoms in newborns if taken during the last months of pregnancy. If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor, as ziprasidone may pass into breast milk. Children and teenagers: this medicine may be prescribed to teens (age 10 and older) for certain conditions — parents should watch carefully for any unusual behavior or mood changes. People with heart problems or a history of irregular heartbeat should inform their doctor before starting this medication. People with liver or kidney disease may need special monitoring.
